title: 3 Non-AI Stocks to Buy for Long-Term Dividends and Stability - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil, McDonald's, and Realty Income are solid income stocks that pay more than double the S&P 500 average These stocks make for stable long-term investments, and they have limited exposure to artificial intelligence and related tech trends. Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are struggling, as investors appear to be having second thoughts about inflated valuations. Anthropic’sstock had a strong first day of trading, but since then it's been struggling. Space Exploration Technologies Corp, another AI stock that went public this year, has also been falling in recent weeks and is trading below its IPO price. Many investors may be growing concerned about all the exposure to AI. However, there are still excellent stocks to consider that have limited or no exposure to AI. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), McDonald's (NYSE:MCD), and Realty Income (NYSE:O) are excellent blue chip dividend stocks that aren't heavily investing in AI and can be relatively stable investments to hold on to, and which can generate tremendous dividend income over the long haul. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Here's a look at why these stocks may be worth buying right now. ExxonMobil's business centers around exploring and producing crude oil and natural gas. While the company has integrated AI into its business to improve efficiency, it's largely the price of oil, rather than AI-related sentiment, that will move the stock. And with oil prices reaching multi-year highs, the stock has been on a tear this year, rising 32% and outperforming the S&P 500, which is up just 5%. An added incentive to buy the oil and gas stock is that it has raised its payout for decades, and even after its strong rally this year, its yield remains relatively high at 2.7%. By comparison, the average S&P 500 stock pays about 1.1%. As a leading company in the oil and gas sector, ExxonMobil can make for an ideal stock to invest in today, especially with oil prices remaining elevated and the war in Iran looking like it'll extend into next year. Another solid stock to own for safety and dividends is McDonald's. The fast-food giant is deploying AI to help determine prices in various markets. While finding what it calls "the optimal price" based on location may be a bit controversial, it's an example of how AI may enable McDonald's to squeeze out more revenue. But like with Exxon, its core business remains unchanged. AI might help McDonald's strengthen its margins, but its success will hinge on its ability to deliver quality meals for consumers while keeping prices relatively low. It's done an excellent job of that over the years, and it's a reason why the stock may be a solid investment, even if there's a downturn in the economy, as its low-cost meal options could be attractive for budget-conscious customers. At 2.8%, McDonald's also pays a fairly high dividend. This year, it also joined the ranks of Dividend Kings, as it extended its dividend growth streak to 50 years. For long-term investors, McDonald's can be a no-brainer stock to hang on to. Realty Income is the final stock on this list, and it's yet another example of a business that can be a suitable option for long-term investors who don't want to worry about AI. It's a real estate investment trust (REIT) that has a diverse mix of clients, so inevitably there may be some exposure to AI, but it isn't likely to be significant. As of the end of September, the industries that accounted for the highest percentage of its annualized base rent were grocery, convenience stores, home improvement, dollar stores, and quick-service restaurants. Those five areas accounted for about 37%. And when strictly looking at data centers, only four properties fell into that category, compared with a total of 15,536 properties in its entire portfolio. The REIT pays the highest dividend on this list, as it currently yields 5.6%. It also makes payments every month and has been increasing its dividend for decades. It's a solid stock for income investors to buy and hold. title: Your Exxon Dividend Needs Only About $59 Oil - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire? Oil has fallen, and oil stocks have fallen with it. WTI crude, the main U.S. oil price, fell 17.3% from $108.21 on Oct 16 to $89.53 on Nov 17. Exxon Mobil stock fell 14.4% in the month to Monday’s close. Chevron fell 11.6%. So what oil price do their payouts actually need? On each company’s own record since 2015, Exxon’s dividend and share buybacks together need WTI to average about $79 a barrel over a year. Chevron’s need about $80. The dividend alone needs much less. That line is about $59 for Exxon and about $65 for Chevron. Oil’s latest print is 12.9% above Exxon’s full-payout line. It is 11.3% above Chevron’s. On this measure, both payouts are still covered. Our read is that the dividends are the safe part, and the buybacks are what cheaper oil would test. Free cash flow is the cash a company keeps after paying for its wells, plants and other capital spending. In the four quarters to September, oil averaged $78.87 a barrel. That is close to the full-payout lines above, about $79 for Exxon and $80 for Chevron. In those months, Exxon’s free cash flow covered its dividend 2.5 times. Its dividends plus buybacks used 87.9% of free cash flow. Chevron’s payouts used 73.3%. Exxon Mobil’s cash covered its quarterly checks to holders 2.5 times over the past year, even as the stock fell 14.4% in a month. If those checks pay your bills, the falling share price is the part you have to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays. The table below runs the same test on four large U.S. producers, next to each stock’s fall over the past month. All cash figures cover the four quarters from October 2025 to September 2026. Price changes run from the Oct 23 close to the Nov 23 close, price only. ConocoPhillips is the thinnest of the four. Its payouts used 95.5% of free cash flow. EOG Resources covered its dividend 3.4 times, the widest margin in the group. The Energy Select Sector SPDR fund, which holds many of these names, fell 13.6% over the same month. The wider market did not drive Monday’s selling. The SPDR S&P 500 fund rose 4.7% that day, while Exxon fell 1.9%. We set each company’s free cash flow for every calendar year from 2015 to 2025 against that year’s average WTI price. A straight line fits Exxon’s record closely. Each $1 a barrel was worth about $1 billion of Exxon’s yearly free cash flow. For Chevron, each $1 was worth about $714 million. We then found the yearly oil price at which that cash equals the latest twelve months of payouts. A check on 47 single quarters gives nearly the same lines. It puts Exxon’s full-payout line at $78.34 and Chevron’s at $78.08. Today’s companies did better than the old record predicts. At the past four quarters’ $78.87 oil, the fit expected $37.3 billion of free cash flow from Exxon. Exxon produced $43 billion. The fit expected $23.9 billion from Chevron, and Chevron produced $34.1 billion. So the lines above are, if anything, on the high side. For how large Exxon’s cash is next to its share price, see Should You Buy Exxon Mobil Stock For Its Cash? For the same test on Chevron, see Should You Buy Chevron Stock For Its Cash? The twelve-month average hides when the cash arrived. 82.6% of Exxon’s free cash flow came in the April to September quarters. For Chevron the share was 88.3%. Oil averaged $95.65 and $87.11 in those two quarters. A year earlier, oil averaged $68.17. At that price, Exxon’s dividends plus buybacks were 159.5% of its free cash flow. Chevron’s were 167.4%. The gap had to come from the balance sheet. From 2015 to 2025, Exxon’s cash covered its dividend in 7 of 11 years. It covered the full payout in only 5. Chevron covered its dividend in 7 years and the full payout in 4. Exxon raised its dividend per share 4% on its latest quarterly call. Management said that was its 44th straight year of growth in the dividend per share. Asked about buybacks at $60 oil, Exxon’s chief executive answered on the dividend. “We’re not going to ever cut our dividend,” he said. The buyback is less firm. Exxon plans to keep buybacks at $20 billion in 2027, “assuming reasonable market conditions”. Chevron said it has kept buybacks at a rate of $2.5 billion to $3 billion a quarter and intends to stay in that range. Two smaller producers state their own lines, measured differently from ours: The test is the yearly average, not one day’s print. So far this quarter, WTI has averaged $98.76, well above both lines. If oil instead averaged below about $80 for a year, we think buybacks would be the first thing to shrink. The dividends look safe on this record down to about $59 for Exxon and $65 for Chevron. Our read: the recent fall prices in more risk to the dividends than the cash shows. The buybacks are the part that needs oil to average above about $80. title: ExxonMobil Holdings (XOM) Stock: Shares Slide 1.62% as Company Unveils $3B Debt Buyback Results - Blockonomi
content: ExxonMobil Holdings (XOM) shares declined 1.62% to $157.40, losing $2.59 as selling pressure erased earlier gains. The stock briefly approached $161.70 before retreating toward intraday lows during the trading session. Meanwhile, ExxonMobil announced results from its $3 billion debt repurchase program involving four outstanding note series. ExxonMobil disclosed the pricing terms and final tender results for debt repurchases conducted through two subsidiaries. Pioneer Natural Resources Company and Exxon Mobil Corporation managed separate cash offers covering their respective outstanding notes. The companies launched the offers on November 16, 2026, with a combined repurchase limit of $3 billion. However, total eligible submissions remained below the maximum amount, allowing both subsidiaries to accept every valid tender. Consequently, neither company needed to reduce accepted amounts through proportional allocations across the four note series. The accepted principal totaled approximately $1.76 billion, covering debt obligations with maturities ranging from 2030 through 2040. The transaction includes two Pioneer note series and two Exxon note series with different interest rates. Pioneer offered to repurchase its 1.900% senior notes due 2030 and 2.150% senior notes due 2031. Exxon targeted its 3.482% notes due 2030 and 4.227% notes due 2040 under separate offers. Pioneer accepted $128.68 million in notes due 2030 and $97.79 million in notes due 2031. The company established consideration of $896.86 and $892.94 per $1,000 principal amount for those respective securities. Both series carried pricing spreads of 22 and 30 basis points above their reference Treasury yields. Exxon accepted approximately $705.41 million of its 3.482% notes maturing in 2030. The company also accepted $832.68 million of its 4.227% notes scheduled to mature in 2040. Their respective repurchase prices reached $957.85 and $872.59 per $1,000 principal amount, excluding accrued interest. The companies calculated these prices using reference Treasury yields and predetermined spreads for each security. Furthermore, both subsidiaries will pay accrued interest through the day preceding the settlement date. The repurchases reduce outstanding debt principal while requiring cash payments according to the announced tender terms. ExxonMobil shares fell $2.59 during the session, marking a 1.62% decline to $157.40. Earlier buying briefly lifted the stock toward $161.70 before sustained selling reversed those gains. Consequently, XOM finished the reported trading period near its intraday lows despite the company’s debt announcement. The debt repurchases follow ExxonMobil’s acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources, which expanded its Permian Basin operations. That acquisition also brought Pioneer’s existing debt obligations into ExxonMobil’s broader corporate structure. The latest tender program addresses selected outstanding securities rather than the company’s entire debt portfolio. The announced results confirm full acceptance of valid tenders without exceeding the established $3 billion ceiling. Additionally, the final accepted amount leaves approximately $1.24 billion below the maximum authorized principal amount. XOM’s share decline accompanied the announcement, although the reported trading figures do not establish its underlying cause.
